sentences.text: Petitioner was summoned to face trial for the offences punishable under Sections 420, 447 and 506 read with Section 149 of Indian Penal Code.

2. Heard learned counsel for the petitioner and learned Assistant Public Prosecutor, appearing for the respondent Nos.1 and 2. Perused the record.
3.
The grievance of the petitioner is that the learned Magistrate had taken cognizance against the petitioner on 17.11.2023.

The docket order reads thus:
"Petitioner Counsel is present, and heard.

Perused the petition and case record and satisfied with the reasons mentioned in the petition, hence in the interest of justice,
this petition is allowed"

4. As seen from the said order, the learned Magistrate has not recorded any reasons as to what promted the learned Magistrate to take cognizance against the petitioner and how the offences are prima facie made out against him.

In the event of any protest petition being filed or any complaint filed against any accused who are not charge sheeted, the procedure to be followed by the learned Magistrate is under Section 200 of Cr.P.C.

No statements were recorded and only on the basis of the FIR and the other statements filed along with the charge sheet under Section 173 of Cr.P.C,
summons were issued to the petitioner.
Issuance of summons in a criminal case is a serious issue and without giving reasons, the petitioner cannot be summoned to face criminal trial.
5. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Sunil Bharti Mittal v. Central Bureau of Investigation 1 held that the order of issuing process to accused to face criminal trial is a serious issue.

entities.text: Sunil Bharti Mittal v. Central Bureau of Investigation 1
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Such summoning cannot be done on mere asking and the Court has to record reasons for summoning a person.

In GHCL Employees Stock Option Trust v. India (2015) 4 Supreme Court Cases 609 Infoline Limited 2, the Hon'ble Supreme Court found fault with the order of the Magistrate in issuing summons when the Magistrate has not recorded his satisfaction about the prima facie case against the accused.

entities.text: GHCL Employees Stock Option Trust v. India (2015) 4 Supreme Court Cases 609 Infoline Limited 2
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
In Chief Enforcement Officer v. Videocon International Limited 3, the Hon'ble Supreme Court while discussing the expression 'cognizance' held that in criminal law 'cognizance'
means becoming aware of and the word used with respect to Court or a Judge initiating proceedings in respect of an offence.

Taking cognizance would involve application of mind by the Magistrate to V.Surender Reddy vs The Station House Officer, on 16 December, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/10487012/
1 the suspected commission of an offence.
6.

sentences.text:
In Fakhruddin Ahmad v. State of Uttaranchal and another 4 it is held as follows:
"17.Nevertheless, it is well settled that before a Magistrate can be said to have taken cognizance of an offence, it is imperative that he must have taken notice of the accusations and applied his mind to the allegations made in the complaint or in the police report or the information received from a source other than a police report, as the case may be, and the material filed therewith.

entities.text: Fakhruddin Ahmad v. State of Uttaranchal and another 4
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
It needs little emphasis that it is only when the Magistrate applies his mind and is satisfied that (2013) 4 SCC 505 (2008) 2 SCC 492 (2008) 17 Supreme Court Cases 157 the allegations, if proved,
would constitute an offence and decides to initiate proceedings against the alleged offender, that it can be positively stated that he has taken cognizance of the offence.

Cognizance is in regard to the offence and not the offender"
7.

In view of the observations and directions of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the judgments referred to supra, the act of issuing process and summoning the accused to face criminal trial is a serious issue and such orders directing summons to a person to face criminal trial cannot be on the basis of cryptic orders and it should be an order reflecting application of mind by the Presiding Officer while taking cognizance and issuing process.
8. Though elaborate discussion is not required for the purpose of issuing summons, the order taking cognizance should reflect that the Presiding Officer has grasp of the case.

The contents of either the charge sheet/private complaint/protest petition are understood by the Presiding Officer and the cognizance orders should reflect that there is a prima facie case stating facts very precisely to summon the accused or refer a case for the purpose of investigation or set aside the findings of investigation and summon the accused.
9. Judicial orders cannot be cryptic or vague or bald assertion that an offence is made out.

It would not suffice to merely mention that cognizance is taken or that mere mentioning that the Presiding Officer is satisfied on the basis of the record that it is a fit case to take cognizance and issue summons.

When the order does not reflect even briefly what the case is about, it is apparent that the Presiding Officer has not applied his mind judicially to the facts of the case before summoning the accused to face criminal trial and the orders are mechanically passed without even considering whether the allegations or the contents of such charge sheets/complaints make out a prima facie case.

10. Since the order dated 17.11.2023 passed by the learned Magistrate lacks reasons and it does not appear that the learned Magistrate has applied mind in issuance of summons, the same is liable to be set aside.

11. Accordingly, the Criminal Petition is allowed and the order dated 17.11.2023 passed in Crl.M.P.No.1305 of 2023 in C.C.No.1391 of 2017 by the learned XIV Additional Metropolitan Magistrate, Ranga Reddy District at Hayathnagar, is hereby set aside.
